content: Neurocysticercosis is a parasitic infection of the central nervous system caused by the larval stage of the pork tapeworm, Taenia solium. It is a significant cause of seizures and epilepsy in regions where the disease is endemic. Anthelmintic drugs, such as albendazole or praziquantel, are often administered alongside supportive treatments like antiepileptic medications or analgesics to target and kill the larval cysts (cysticerci). Corticosteroids may also be used in conjunction with these treatments. However, these drugs can cause adverse effects, and in some cases, the cysticerci may die naturally without specific anthelmintic therapy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of anthelmintic treatment in individuals with neurocysticercosis. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, the WHO ICTRP, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to October 21, 2020. They included randomized controlled trials that compared anthelmintic therapy combined with supportive treatment (with or without corticosteroids) to supportive treatment alone (with or without corticosteroids). Two authors independently screened the titles and abstracts of identified studies, retrieved full-text articles for eligible studies, and extracted data. A second author verified the extracted data. The risk of bias for each trial was assessed, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third author. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and data from studies with similar interventions and outcomes were pooled. The review included 16 studies. Only two studies investigated praziquantel, but their data could not be included in the meta-analysis. Therefore, most of the findings pertain to albendazole compared to placebo or no anthelmintic treatment. The pooled analysis of all participants with neurocysticercosis did not show a significant difference in seizure recurrence between the albendazole and control groups (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.14; 10 trials, 1054 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, there was substantial heterogeneity (I² = 67%). When the data were stratified by the number of cysts, albendazole appeared to reduce seizure recurrence in participants with a single cyst (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.91; 5 trials, 396 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). All studies contributing to this analysis included participants with non-viable, intraparenchymal cysts, and most participants were children. For participants with multiple cysts, the evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether albendazole reduces seizure recurrence. In fact, the direction of the effect suggested potential harm (RR 2.05, 95% CI 1.28 to 3.31; 2 trials, 321 participants; very low-certainty evidence). This analysis included a large, heterogeneous study with unclear risk of bias in several domains. Regarding radiological outcomes, albendazole likely improves the complete clearance of lesions on imaging (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.39; 13 trials, 1324 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and promotes the evolution of cysts (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.47; 6 trials, 434 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Participants treated with albendazole or praziquantel experienced more adverse events compared to those receiving placebo or no anthelmintic treatment. The most frequently reported side effects were headache, abdominal pain, and nausea or vomiting. In conclusion, for individuals with a single non-viable intraparenchymal cyst, albendazole was associated with a reduction in seizure recurrence compared to placebo or no anthelmintic treatment. However, the evidence is uncertain regarding its effects on seizure recurrence in individuals with multiple cysts. Albendazole likely improves radiological outcomes, including lesion clearance and cyst evolution. There were limited data on praziquantel, so these findings primarily apply to albendazole.
